description:
We are a multidisciplinary team comprising Telecommunication Engineering (UniKL BMI) and Aerospace Engineering (UniKL MIAT) students alongside a geologist at GMTGeos.

For NASA Space Apps 2026, we are tackling Dancing with the SARs, exploring how satellite radar and geospatial data can reveal changes on Earth's surface.

We aim to build an accessible solution and welcome members skilled in Python, GIS/QGIS, remote sensing, data visualization and web development.
summary:
Pengerang EarthWatch: Seeing What the Clouds Hide

Pengerang EarthWatch is an interactive geospatial application developed by Team Artemis Gema to investigate land-surface changes associated with peatland disturbances in Pengerang, Johor, Malaysia, where a major fire affected approximately 51.4 hectares in August 2026.

Using real ESA Copernicus Sentinel-1 C-band Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) observations acquired on 23 August and 4 September 2026, our team developed a reproducible workflow for visualizing calibrated VH-polarized radar backscatter and calculating temporal changes.

Built using Python, FastAPI, Rasterio, and Leaflet, the application enables users to explore satellite imagery, interactively compare observations through a before-and-after slider, adjust visualization layers, and examine radar backscatter differences.

Aligned with the Dancing with the SARs challenge's emphasis on interactive Earth observation, EarthWatch makes complex radar information more accessible and understandable.

While radar changes alone cannot confirm fire damage, our prototype demonstrates how open satellite data can support environmental investigations and provides a foundation for future integration of NASA NISAR observations and additional validation datasets.
details:
Pengerang EarthWatch - Project Details

1. Project Overview

Pengerang EarthWatch is an interactive geospatial monitoring application developed by Team Artemis Gema for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, under the Dancing with the SARs challenge.

Our project addresses the difficulty of observing and interpreting environmental surface changes in tropical regions, using the August 2026 peatland fire in Pengerang, Johor, Malaysia, as a real-world case study. The incident affected approximately 51.4 hectares of peatland, highlighting the need for accessible satellite-based environmental monitoring.

Unlike conventional optical satellite imagery, Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) can acquire observations during both day and night and through cloud cover. We use this capability to investigate land-surface changes across different observation dates.

2. How Our Application Works

EarthWatch follows a three-stage approach: Observe, Investigate, and Understand.

Observe: Users explore georeferenced Sentinel-1 C-band SAR imagery through an interactive map. Our application uses calibrated VH-polarized radar observations acquired on 23 August and 4 September 2026, representing periods before and after the documented fire event.

Investigate: Users can switch observation dates, interactively swipe between satellite images, adjust layer opacity, and examine changes in radar backscatter. Our processing workflow calculates the difference between post-event and pre-event VH measurements, expressed in decibels (dB).

Understand: The application provides explanatory information about the radar observations and their limitations. Users can investigate surface-change patterns while recognizing that changes in radar backscatter may result from vegetation, soil moisture, surface roughness, or other environmental factors.

The platform does not automatically classify burned areas or attribute every radar change to fire.

3. Technologies and Development Tools

Our prototype combines open satellite data with geospatial processing and web development technologies.

  • Satellite Data: ESA Copernicus Sentinel-1D C-band SAR, VH polarization.
  • Data Acquisition: Google Earth Engine for accessing calibrated, terrain-corrected SAR imagery.
  • Programming Languages: Python, JavaScript, HTML, and CSS.
  • Backend: FastAPI and Uvicorn for application services and data delivery.
  • Geospatial Processing: Rasterio and NumPy for processing GeoTIFF imagery and calculating radar backscatter differences.
  • Frontend: Leaflet for interactive geographic visualization and image comparisons.
  • Data Format: Georeferenced GeoTIFF raster files, exported at 20-metre pixel spacing.
  • Collaboration and Reproducibility: GitHub for source-code sharing and project documentation.

Our current implementation operates as a locally hosted web application and uses actual satellite observations rather than simulated radar measurements.

4. Creativity and Innovation

EarthWatch transforms technical SAR datasets into an accessible interactive investigation experience.

Instead of presenting static satellite images, users can directly compare observations, examine temporal changes, and adjust how radar information is displayed.

Our innovation lies in combining interactive visualization, reproducible geospatial analysis, and transparent scientific interpretation within one application.

We deliberately distinguish satellite-observed changes from confirmed fire damage. This approach promotes responsible communication of environmental information and reduces the risk of misleading conclusions.

5. Intended Benefits and Impact

EarthWatch aims to make satellite-based environmental monitoring more accessible to researchers, students, environmental agencies, land managers, and local communities.

Its potential benefits include improved understanding of radar-based surface observations, easier comparison of environmental conditions across time, and greater awareness of peatland monitoring challenges.

The platform also provides an educational demonstration of how SAR technology can support investigations in tropical regions where persistent cloud cover limits optical observations.

Our longer-term vision is to expand this approach to other environmentally sensitive areas across Malaysia and Southeast Asia.

6. Scientific Considerations and Future Development

During development, our team prioritized data authenticity, reproducibility, consistent acquisition geometry, accessibility, and scientific transparency.

We selected Sentinel-1 observations from the same descending relative orbit to support a more consistent temporal comparison. We also retained the original numerical radar measurements in GeoTIFF format.

However, our study-area boundary has not been independently confirmed as the actual burned perimeter. Consequently, the detected radar changes should not be interpreted as verified fire damage.

Although our current prototype uses ESA Sentinel-1 data, our next development objective is to integrate NASA NISAR L-band observations and complementary datasets such as NASA FIRMS for broader environmental evidence assessment.

Ultimately, Pengerang EarthWatch demonstrates how interactive geospatial technology can transform complex radar observations into understandable information, establishing a foundation for more accessible, transparent, and evidence-based environmental monitoring.
